args.query: What operation combines the shortcut connection with the residual branch in an identity block in the original ResNet?
Which layer outputs does a DenseNet layer receive inside a dense block?
What direct architectural implication follows from ResNet using addition versus DenseNet using concatenation?

args.instructions: Answer the question directly in the first sentence. Then compare what each paper says, naming the paper for every point, and state where the papers agree, disagree or report numbers that are not comparable. If one hop of the question is not answered by the evidence, say which.

result.answer: Answer: ResNet identity blocks combine the shortcut with the residual branch by element-wise addition, y = F(x, {Wi}) + x [S:43eecbafc161#21][S:43eecbafc161#22]; DenseNet layers inside a dense block take all preceding feature-maps as input and concatenate them [S:20e50960076d#8][S:20e50960076d#69]. One direct architectural implication is that DenseNet cannot simply concatenate when feature-map sizes change, so it divides the network into dense blocks separated by transition layers [S:20e50960076d#28].

claims.text: In the original ResNet, a building block is defined as y = F(x, {Wi}) + x, with F the residual mapping to be learned.
claims.note: Span explicitly defines building block y = F(x, {Wi}) + x and F as residual mapping.

claims.text: ResNet performs the F + x operation by a shortcut connection and element-wise addition.
claims.note: Span states F + x is performed by shortcut connection and element-wise addition.

claims.text: ResNet requires x and F to have equal dimensions, and applies a linear projection Ws through the shortcut when they differ.
claims.note: Span says x and F dimensions must be equal, and linear projection Ws is used when not.

claims.text: DenseNet's dense block takes all preceding feature-maps as input.
claims.note: Caption says each layer in dense block takes all preceding feature-maps as input.

claims.text: DenseNet uses input concatenation to combine features.
claims.note: Span explicitly refers to DenseNet's input concatenation and feature reuse.

claims.text: As a direct consequence of input concatenation, feature-maps learned by any DenseNet layer can be accessed by all subsequent layers.
claims.note: Span directly states this exact consequence of input concatenation.

claims.text: DenseNet's input concatenation encourages feature reuse and leads to more compact models.
claims.note: Span states input concatenation encourages feature reuse and leads to more compact models.

claims.text: DenseNet's concatenation operation is not viable when feature-map size changes, so DenseNet divides the network into dense blocks with transition layers.
claims.note: Span says concatenation is not viable when feature-map size changes and describes dense blocks plus transition layers for down-sampling.

citations.text:
3.2. Identity Mapping by Shortcuts
We adopt residual learning to every few stacked layers.
A building block is shown in Fig. 2. Formally, in this paper
we consider a building block deﬁned as:
y = F(x, {Wi}) + x.
(1)
Here x and y are the input and output vectors of the lay-
ers considered.
The function F(x, {Wi}) represents the
residual mapping to be learned. For the example in Fig. 2
that has two layers, F = W2σ(W1x) in which σ denotes
2This hypothesis, however, is still an open question. See [28].

citations.title: arXiv:1512.03385v1  [cs.CV]  10 Dec 2015
citations.text:
ReLU [29] and the biases are omitted for simplifying no-
tations. The operation F + x is performed by a shortcut
connection and element-wise addition. We adopt the sec-
ond nonlinearity after the addition (i.e., σ(y), see Fig. 2).
The shortcut connections in Eqn.(1) introduce neither ex-
tra parameter nor computation complexity. This is not only
attractive in practice but also important in our comparisons
between plain and residual networks. We can fairly com-
pare plain/residual networks that simultaneously have the
same number of parameters, depth, width, and computa-
tional cost (except for the negligible element-wise addition).
The dimensions of x and F must be equal in Eqn.(1).
If this is not the case (e.g., when changing the input/output
channels), we can perform a linear projection Ws by the
shortcut connections to match the dimensions:
y = F(x, {Wi}) + Wsx.

citations.text:
Model compactness.
As a direct consequence of the in-
put concatenation, the feature-maps learned by any of the
DenseNet layers can be accessed by all subsequent layers.
This encourages feature reuse throughout the network, and
leads to more compact models.
The left two plots in Figure 4 show the result of an
experiment that aims to compare the parameter efﬁciency
of all variants of DenseNets (left) and also a comparable

citations.title: arXiv:1608.06993v5  [cs.CV]  28 Jan 2018
citations.text:
Pooling layers.
The concatenation operation used in
Eq. (2) is not viable when the size of feature-maps changes.
However, an essential part of convolutional networks is
down-sampling layers that change the size of feature-maps.
To facilitate down-sampling in our architecture we divide
the network into multiple densely connected dense blocks;
see Figure 2. We refer to layers between blocks as transition
layers, which do convolution and pooling. The transition
layers used in our experiments consist of a batch normal-
ization layer and an 1×1 convolutional layer followed by a
2×2 average pooling layer.
